When you become a manager, your job changes in one important way: you are now measured by what your team achieves, not by what you produce yourself. Many new managers keep doing the work they were good at, because it feels productive. The result is a busy manager and an under-used team.

## Your three jobs

- Make the goal clear: everyone should know what good looks like and why it matters.
- Remove obstacles: unblock decisions, resources and conflicts your team cannot solve alone.
- Grow people: give each person work that stretches them, and feedback that helps them improve.

## Building trust early

Trust grows when people see you do what you say. In your first weeks, meet each team member, ask what helps them do good work and what gets in the way, and act on at least one thing you heard. Be honest about what you don't know yet. Avoid changing everything at once: understand why things are done a certain way before you change them.

## Delegating well

Delegation is not dumping tasks. Good delegation agrees four things up front: the outcome (what finished looks like), the deadline, the decision authority (what they can decide alone and what needs your input), and the check-in points. Match the level of support to the person's experience with that task: a new task needs closer check-ins than one they have done many times.

## In practice

A supervisor in a distribution company used to prepare the weekly stock report herself every Friday. She delegated it to a team member by showing one finished example, agreeing the Thursday-evening deadline, saying he could correct small data errors himself but should flag differences above 5%, and checking the first two reports together. By week four she only reviewed the summary.

## Common mistakes

- Taking work back at the first problem, which teaches people to wait for you.
- Delegating only boring tasks, never interesting ones.
- Giving responsibility without the authority or information to deliver it.

## Try it

List three tasks you still do that someone in your team could learn. For one of them, write the outcome, deadline, decision authority and check-in points you would agree.

A team works hard on the wrong things when priorities are vague. Your job is to turn broad direction from above into a small number of clear goals your team can act on.

## Fewer, clearer goals

Most teams can focus on three to five goals at a time. More than that and everything becomes a priority, which means nothing is. Ask: if we only achieved three things this quarter, which three would matter most?

## Make goals specific and measurable

A useful goal says what will change, by how much, and by when. "Improve customer service" is a wish. "Answer 90% of customer emails within 24 hours by the end of March" is a goal. Each goal also needs one clear owner: shared ownership often means no ownership.

## Connect goals to the bigger picture

People commit more when they understand why a goal matters. Explain how the team goal supports the company's targets, and how each person's work contributes. If you can't explain why a goal matters, question whether it should be a goal.

## Saying no

Setting priorities means deciding what you will not do. When a new request arrives, compare it with current goals: does it matter more than something already planned? If yes, agree what will be delayed. If no, explain why it waits.

## In practice

A sales team had eleven targets. The manager reduced them to four (new accounts, repeat orders, overdue invoices and visit reports), wrote each as a number with a deadline, and named an owner for each. Weekly meetings shrank from ninety minutes to thirty because everyone knew what to report.

## Common mistakes

- Writing activities ("make calls") instead of outcomes ("sign 5 new accounts").
- Changing priorities every week, so nothing is finished.
- Setting goals without checking the team has the time and resources.

## Try it

Take one vague goal your team has today and rewrite it with a measurable result, a deadline and one owner.

A one-to-one (1:1) is a regular private meeting between a manager and one team member. Done well, it is where problems surface early, trust grows and people develop. Done badly, it becomes a status update that could have been an email.

## It is their meeting

The best 1:1s are led by the team member's agenda: what they want to discuss, what is blocking them, how they are doing. Your role is mainly to listen and ask good questions. Status updates on tasks belong in team meetings or shared trackers.

## A simple structure

- Their topics first: what's on your mind this week?
- Obstacles: what's slowing you down, and what can I do about it?
- Development: what do you want to get better at, and what would help?
- Agreements: what will each of us do before next time?

## Rhythm and reliability

Hold 1:1s at a regular rhythm (weekly or every two weeks) and protect them. Cancelling repeatedly tells people they are not a priority. If you must move one, reschedule it straight away rather than skipping it.

## Listening well

Ask open questions ("How is the new process working for you?") rather than yes/no questions. Let silences last a few seconds; people often say the important thing after a pause. Take brief notes of agreements so you can follow up.

## In practice

A warehouse team leader kept a shared document for each person with three headings: their topics, actions agreed, and development goals. Before each 1:1 the team member added topics. After a few weeks, two people raised safety concerns in their 1:1s that they had never mentioned in group meetings.

## Common mistakes

- Turning the 1:1 into a list of your instructions.
- Only holding 1:1s when something is wrong.
- Forgetting what was agreed last time.

## Try it

Prepare three open questions you could ask in your next 1:1 that are not about task status.

Feedback is information about the effect of someone's behaviour, given so they can keep doing what works and change what doesn't. Good feedback is specific, timely and focused on behaviour, not personality.

## Describe behaviour and impact

A reliable pattern is: situation, behaviour, impact. Say when it happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. For example: "In this morning's client meeting, you interrupted the client twice while they were explaining the problem. They stopped sharing details, and we left without the information we needed." This is far more useful than "You're rude in meetings."

## Then make it two-way

After describing the behaviour and impact, ask for their view: "How did you see it?" There may be context you don't know. Then agree together what to do differently next time.

## Timing and balance

Give feedback soon, while the details are fresh, and in private when it is corrective. Positive feedback matters as much as corrective feedback: telling people specifically what they did well makes it more likely they repeat it. Make feedback a regular habit, not an annual event.

## Receiving feedback

Ask your team for feedback on your own management, and react calmly when you get it. Thank the person, ask questions to understand, and show what you changed. People give honest feedback to managers who visibly use it.

## In practice

A finance supervisor noticed a colleague's month-end reconciliations were accurate but always late. Instead of saying "you're slow", she said: "The last two reconciliations arrived on the 6th instead of the 3rd, which delayed the management report. What's getting in the way?" The colleague explained he was waiting for bank statements; they agreed he would request them earlier.

## Common mistakes

- Labelling the person ("lazy", "careless") instead of describing what they did.
- Saving feedback for the annual review.
- Hiding the real message between two compliments.

## Try it

Write one piece of positive and one piece of corrective feedback for someone you work with, using situation, behaviour and impact.

When a team member brings you a problem, the quickest response is to tell them the answer. Do that every time, and your team learns to bring you every problem. Coaching means helping people find their own solutions, so they grow and you are no longer the bottleneck.

## When to coach and when to tell

Coach when the person has the knowledge or experience to work it out, and there is time. Tell when there is a safety risk, an urgent deadline, or the person genuinely lacks the information. Most everyday problems are coaching opportunities.

## Questions that help

- What's the situation, and what have you tried so far?
- What outcome do you want?
- What options do you see?
- What are the risks of each option?
- What will you do first, and when?

Ask one question at a time and let the person think. Resist the urge to hint at your preferred answer.

## Ownership stays with them

The aim is for the person to leave owning the decision and the next step. If their plan is reasonable but different from what you would do, let them try it: they will learn more from their own approach, and you may learn something too. Step in only if the risk is too high.

## In practice

A new customer service agent asked her manager how to handle a customer demanding a refund outside policy. Instead of answering, the manager asked what the policy allowed, what the customer really needed, and what options she had. She proposed a replacement product instead of a refund, which the customer accepted. Next time, she solved a similar case alone.

## Common mistakes

- Asking questions while clearly steering towards your own answer.
- Coaching in a crisis when the person needs a direct instruction.
- Taking the problem back at the end ("leave it with me").

## Try it

The next time someone brings you a problem, ask at least three of the questions above before offering any suggestion.

Agreeing goals and actions is only half the job. Accountability means people do what they committed to, and when they don't, the reasons are discussed openly and fairly. It is built through clear agreements and consistent follow-up, not through pressure.

## Make agreements clear

Every action needs an owner, a deliverable and a date. End meetings by reading back who will do what by when. Write it down in a place everyone can see. Vague agreements ("let's look into it") are almost never completed.

## Follow up consistently

Check progress at the agreed points, not randomly. Use the same tracker or meeting slot each time so follow-up becomes routine rather than personal. When you forget to follow up, people learn that deadlines are optional.

## When commitments are missed

Start with curiosity, not blame: "The report was due Tuesday and I haven't seen it. What happened?" There may be a real obstacle you can remove. Then agree a new date and what will be different. If the same commitment is missed repeatedly, treat it as a performance conversation: describe the pattern, its impact, and what must change.

## Hold yourself accountable too

Teams copy their manager. If you meet your own commitments, admit when you miss one and say how you will fix it, people are far more likely to do the same.

## In practice

A logistics manager introduced a five-minute review at the start of each weekly meeting: the team looked at last week's action list, each owner said done, late or blocked, and blocked items got help. Within a month, on-time completion of agreed actions rose noticeably, and nobody felt singled out because everyone followed the same routine.

## Common mistakes

- Agreeing actions without owners or dates.
- Following up only with people you are unhappy with.
- Ignoring missed commitments, then reacting angrily months later.

## Try it

At your next team meeting, end by reading back every action with its owner and date, and put them in one shared list.
